tier_reason: ch4/1_primes/primes.cu times the GPU kernel (CUDA events) against a single-threaded CPU loop (std::chrono) and prints the speedup, but no repo page shows results, flags or hardware; the 1.23x/9.66x/67.91x figures are the book's own run, so first-party C, and the cap at C applies anyway (no flags in CMakeLists.txt, gain above 50x, host loop probably unoptimised).

corrections.caveats: Probably not a valid measurement; candidate for the MQF no-op precedent if a build confirms it. By reading the source (not compiled or run; no CUDA toolchain here): checkPrimeKernel keeps its result in a local bool isPrime that is never stored or printed (the printf is commented out), so the kernel has no observable effect and nvcc's device optimiser (on by default) may delete the trial-division loop; the GPU time of 0.2298 ms for the largest range could then be mostly launch overhead. The timed GPU region also contains the process's first kernel launch with no warm-up (module loading can land there). The CPU result of checkPrimeCpu is discarded too: the 15.6 ms CPU time suggests the host loop was not optimised, since an optimising build would likely remove the discarded calls, so the baseline is a probable -O0-style loop on one core against a GPU build that is optimised by default. Speedup rising roughly in step with range size (1.23x, 9.66x, 67.91x) is what a near-constant GPU time against a linear CPU time gives. Nothing checks that GPU and CPU results agree. The repo holds only the 100,001 to 190,001 range; the other two ranges were presumably produced by editing the 'end' constant. No memory transfers are involved. ch4/1_primes/CMakeLists.txt sets no flags and no build type, and ch4/readme.md says only 'cmake ..' then 'make'. Numbers, CPU and GPU models come only from the book. Last commit 2025-12-15 is a README banner change; the last code change is 2025-08-20. Capped at C: speedup above 50x with unstated flags, first-party.

notes: Kernel result never stored (confirmed on the blob page), so the GPU timing may measure an empty kernel; unproven without an nvcc build, so kept at C with the defect documented instead of rejected. tier_reason: ch4/2_vector_add/vector_add.cu (N = 100,000,000, 1024 threads per block) times copies and kernel with CUDA events and the CPU loop with std::chrono, printing kernel-only and total speedups, but no repo page shows results, flags or hardware; the 44.04x and 1.02x figures are the book's own run, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: The headline 44.04x is kernel-only and excludes the two host-to-device copies and the device-to-host copy, which the same program shows cost almost all of the time (end-to-end 1.02x, i.e. no net gain). The host buffers come from malloc (pageable, not pinned), so the copy times are larger than pinned transfers would give. The CPU baseline is one scalar loop on one core, and ch4/2_vector_add/CMakeLists.txt sets no flags and no build type (ch4/readme.md says only 'cmake ..' then 'make'), so it is probably unoptimised; 1.2 GB of traffic in 218.270 ms is about 5.5 GB/s (derived from the relayed book numbers), low for a vectorised memory-bound loop. Not compared with std::transform under a parallel policy or a vectorised loop. No correctness check: vectorAddCpu writes into the same h_C that received the GPU result, so the GPU output is overwritten unchecked. Single run, no warm-up: the timed kernel is the process's first launch. The book's 10-thousand-to-100-million sweep is not in the repo (only N = 100,000,000); numbers, compiler flags and the CPU and GPU models come only from the book. Last commit 2025-12-15 is a README banner change; the last code change is 2025-08-20. Tier C: first-party.

notes: Code matches the record. Added pageable-memory copies, the missing correctness check (h_C overwritten by the CPU loop) and the readme build without flags. The headline gain is kernel-only; end to end there is no gain.

tier_reason: ch7/matrix_multiply_float.cu holds the naive, shared-memory and shared+unroll+fmaf kernels (main() launches only matrixMulKernel) and ch7/CMakeLists.txt states Release flags, but the 47.33 ms and 33.37 ms kernel times and the hardware come only from the book's Nsight Compute runs, so first-party C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: ch7/CMakeLists.txt declares only the CUDA language; Release sets CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS_RELEASE '-O3 -arch=sm_75 -rdc=false' (and CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE -O3, which does not apply to the .cu file), Debug sets CUDA '-G -g -O0'. No build type is set in the file and ch7/readme.md says only 'cmake ..' then 'make', so the book's Release figures need -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release. sm_75 matches the RTX 2060 (Turing). Repo README lists g++ 9.4, CUDA Toolkit 12, CMake 3.16 and Nsight Compute 2023.3 as the environment.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the book's own naive kernel, not cuBLAS or any library: 2000^3 x 2 FLOP in 33.37 ms is about 0.48 TFLOP/s (derived from the relayed numbers), far from what a tuned library reaches on the same card. The repo's main() launches only matrixMulKernel; the naive and plain shared kernels are swapped in by editing the file, and the 47.33 ms and 33.37 ms figures come from the book's profiler runs (one run per version), not from any repo file. Two of the named optimisations probably add little: '#pragma unroll' sits on a loop bounded by the runtime blockDim.x, so it cannot be fully unrolled (the TILE constant would allow it), and nvcc already contracts 'sum += a * b' into FMA by default (--fmad=true), so the explicit fmaf likely matches matrixMulKernel_shared in Release; the gain over naive comes from shared-memory tiling. The book's 42% compares times as 47.33/33.37 (speed gain), not as a reduction in time (about 29%). Following the readme ('cmake ..', no build type) builds without the Release flags. A checkResults pass compares the GPU result with a CPU triple loop at an absolute 1e-4 tolerance. Last commit 2025-12-15 is a README banner change; the last code change is 2025-08-20. Tier C: first-party, hardware named only in the book.

notes: Code and flags match the record; added the readme build without a build type, the runtime-bounded unroll and nvcc's default FMA contraction, which make the 'unroll + fmaf' label mostly nominal. A small textbook gain over a naive kernel; no library baseline.
